sine-cosine-values-s1.title: A point on a circle of radius 4
sine-cosine-values-s1.text: The circle $x^2 + y^2 = 16$ is centered at the origin $O$. The point $Q$ is on the circle, on the terminal ray of the angle $\frac{2\pi}{3}$ in standard position.

plot.label: The circle x^2 + y^2 = 16 centered at the origin, with the segment from the origin to the point Q on the circle in the second quadrant, at angle 2 pi over 3

sine-cosine-values-s2.title: A robot arm
sine-cosine-values-s2.text: A robot arm 2 meters long pivots at the origin. Its tip starts on the positive $x$-axis and turns counterclockwise. The table gives the angle $\theta$ the arm has turned, in radians, at four times.

table.caption: Angle $\theta(t)$ turned by the arm, in radians, $t$ seconds after the start

mistakes.why: $Q$ is left of the $y$-axis, so its $x$-coordinate is negative: $4\cos\frac{2\pi}{3} = 4\left(-\frac{1}{2}\right)$.
That is $\cos\frac{2\pi}{3}$ on the unit circle. This circle has radius 4, so multiply by 4.
That uses $\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$ for the cosine. The ray at $\frac{2\pi}{3}$ is closer to the $y$-axis, so the smaller value, $\frac{1}{2}$, goes with $x$.

why.correct: $x = 4\cos\frac{2\pi}{3}$. The reference angle is $\frac{\pi}{3}$ and Quadrant II makes cosine negative: $4\left(-\frac{1}{2}\right) = -2$.

mistakes.why: That is $\sin\frac{2\pi}{3}$ on the unit circle. Multiply by the radius 4.
$Q$ is above the $x$-axis, so its $y$-coordinate is positive.
That uses $\frac{1}{2}$ for the sine. At $\frac{2\pi}{3}$ the ray is closer to the $y$-axis, so the height is the larger value, $\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$, times 4.

items.q: What is the slope of the segment $OQ$?

why.correct: The slope is $\tan\frac{2\pi}{3} = \frac{\sqrt{3}/2}{-1/2} = -\sqrt{3}$; with the coordinates, $\frac{2\sqrt{3}}{-2} = -\sqrt{3}$. The radius does not change the slope.
options: This is $\tan\frac{5\pi}{6}$: it divides $x$ by $y$ instead of $y$ by $x$.
The segment rises to the left, so the slope is negative.
This is $\cos\frac{2\pi}{3}$, a coordinate, not the slope of the ray.

items.q: The point $R$ is on the same circle, on the terminal ray of $\frac{2\pi}{3} + \pi$. What are the coordinates of $R$?

why.correct: Half a turn more points the ray the opposite way, so $R$ is diametrically opposite $Q$: both coordinates change sign, $(2, -2\sqrt{3})$. Check: $\frac{5\pi}{3}$ is in Quadrant IV with reference angle $\frac{\pi}{3}$.
options: This flips only the $y$-coordinate, the reflection across the $x$-axis, which is the angle $\frac{4\pi}{3}$.
This swaps the sizes; with reference angle $\frac{\pi}{3}$ the larger size belongs to $y$.
This is $Q$ itself, the point for a full turn $2\pi$, not half a turn.

items.q: What is the $x$-coordinate of the tip at $t = 1$, in meters?

mistakes.why: That is $\cos\frac{3\pi}{4}$ on the unit circle. The arm is 2 meters long: multiply by 2.
$\frac{3\pi}{4}$ is in Quadrant II, where the $x$-coordinate is negative.

items.q: What is the $y$-coordinate of the tip at $t = 2$, in meters?

mistakes.why: $\frac{7\pi}{6}$ is in Quadrant III, below the $x$-axis, so the height is negative.
That is the $x$-coordinate. With reference angle $\frac{\pi}{6}$, the height uses $\frac{1}{2}$.
That is $\sin\frac{7\pi}{6}$ on the unit circle. Multiply by the arm's length, 2.

why.correct: $\frac{5\pi}{3}$ is in Quadrant IV with reference angle $\frac{\pi}{3}$: $\cos\frac{5\pi}{3} = \frac{1}{2}$, $\sin\frac{5\pi}{3} = -\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$. Times 2: $(1, -\sqrt{3})$.
options: Quadrant IV signs, reference angle $\frac{\pi}{3}$, scaled by 2.
This is Quadrant III. $\frac{5\pi}{3}$ is past $\frac{3\pi}{2}$, so $x > 0$.
This is the point on the unit circle; the arm is 2 meters long.

why.correct: $\frac{11\pi}{4} = 2\pi + \frac{3\pi}{4}$: one full turn and then $\frac{3\pi}{4}$, so the tip is where it was at $t = 1$: $\left(2\cos\frac{3\pi}{4}, 2\sin\frac{3\pi}{4}\right) = (-\sqrt{2}, \sqrt{2})$.
options: Remove the full turn: same point as $\frac{3\pi}{4}$, in Quadrant II.
This is the Quadrant IV point, the angle $\frac{7\pi}{4}$. Subtract $2\pi$ from $\frac{11\pi}{4}$, not $\pi$.
This is the Quadrant III point, the angle $\frac{5\pi}{4}$.
This is the Quadrant I point, $\frac{\pi}{4}$; it keeps the reference angle but drops the sign of $x$.

items.q: What is the exact value of $\sin\frac{5\pi}{4}$?

mistakes.why: $\frac{5\pi}{4}$ is in Quadrant III, below the $x$-axis, so sine is negative.
That is the value for a reference angle of $\frac{\pi}{6}$. The reference angle of $\frac{5\pi}{4}$ is $\frac{\pi}{4}$.

items.q: What is the exact value of $\cos\frac{2\pi}{3}$?

mistakes.why: $\frac{2\pi}{3}$ is in Quadrant II, left of the $y$-axis, so cosine is negative.
The reference angle is $\frac{\pi}{3}$, whose cosine is $\frac{1}{2}$; $\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$ is its sine.

items.q: What is the exact value of $\tan\frac{\pi}{6}$?

options: $\sqrt{3}$ is $\tan\frac{\pi}{3}$: cosine over sine is upside down here.

items.q: What is the reference angle of $\frac{5\pi}{6}$?

why.correct: $\frac{5\pi}{6}$ is in Quadrant II, so its reference angle is $\pi - \frac{5\pi}{6} = \frac{\pi}{6}$, the acute angle to the negative $x$-axis.
options: The ray is $\frac{\pi}{6}$ short of the negative $x$-axis.
$\frac{5\pi}{6} - \frac{\pi}{2} = \frac{\pi}{3}$ measures to the $y$-axis; reference angles are measured to the $x$-axis.
A reference angle is acute, between $0$ and $\frac{\pi}{2}$.
This is the angle half a turn away, not a reference angle.

items.q: Which of these equal $-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$? Select all that apply.

why.correct: Only $\cos\frac{5\pi}{6}$: Quadrant II, reference angle $\frac{\pi}{6}$, negative $x$-coordinate $-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$.
options: Reference angle $\frac{\pi}{6}$, cosine negative in Quadrant II.
$\sin\frac{5\pi}{6} = \frac{1}{2}$: the height uses the smaller value and is positive in Quadrant II.
$\cos\frac{7\pi}{4} = \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}$: reference angle $\frac{\pi}{4}$, positive in Quadrant IV.
$\sin\frac{2\pi}{3} = \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$, positive: Quadrant II is above the $x$-axis.

items.q: What is the exact value of $\tan\frac{3\pi}{4}$?

mistakes.why: The point $\left(-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}, \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\right)$ has coordinates of opposite signs, so the slope is negative.
That is $\cos\frac{3\pi}{4}$. Tangent divides the sine by the cosine.

items.q: A point is on a circle of radius 10 centered at the origin, on the terminal ray of $\frac{\pi}{6}$. What are its coordinates?

options: This is the point at $\frac{\pi}{3}$: the coordinates are swapped.
This is the point on the unit circle; multiply by the radius 10.
This doubles the right answer: $10 \cdot \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} = 5\sqrt{3}$, not $10\sqrt{3}$.

items.q: Put the steps for finding $\cos\frac{4\pi}{3}$ exactly in order.

why.correct: Quadrant, reference angle, first-quadrant value, then the sign: cosine is negative in Quadrant III.
